title: Analysis: Wind and solar power overtake fossil fuels in Germany for first time ever - Carbon Brief
gist: In 2025, wind and solar overtook fossil fuels as Germany's largest power source for the first time (44% vs 43%), a milestone mirrored across the EU, even as the Merz government pushes new gas-fired capacity and faces criticism over proposed grid-connection reforms.

insights.claim: In 2025, wind and solar power generated 225TWh of electricity (44% of Germany's total) versus 217TWh (43%) from fossil fuels, marking the first time renewables overtook fossil fuels as Germany's largest power source.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Confirms a structural crossover point in Germany's power mix, relevant to utilities, grid operators, and renewable-energy investors tracking the pace of the fossil-to-renewables substitution.
insights.quote: 225 terawatt hours (TWh) of electricity – accounting for 44% of the total in 2025 – with just 217TWh (43%) coming from fossil fuels
insights.locator: More of Germany's electricity came from wind and solar

insights.claim: The EU as a whole also saw wind and solar generation overtake fossil-fuel power generation for the first time in 2025, indicating Germany's crossover is part of a broader European trend rather than an isolated national outcome.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Signals bloc-wide tailwinds for renewables developers and equipment suppliers, not just a Germany-specific policy effect.
insights.quote: The success of renewables in Germany mirrors the EU as a whole, which also saw wind and solar overtake fossil-fuel power generation in 2025 for the first time.
insights.locator: The success of renewables in Germany mirrors the EU

insights.claim: Germany's solar and onshore wind capacity has grown rapidly over the past two decades under the 'Energiewende' strategy, as the country simultaneously phases out coal and nuclear power.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The two-decade policy consistency behind renewables growth suggests the trend is structural and less likely to reverse quickly, despite current political friction.
insights.locator: Solar and onshore wind have grown rapidly

insights.claim: Germany aims to raise renewables' share of electricity consumption to 80% by 2030, reach a 'largely climate neutral' power system by 2035, phase out coal no later than 2038, and hit economy-wide net-zero emissions by 2045.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: These dated targets give investors and policymakers concrete milestones to benchmark Germany's actual power-mix progress against.
insights.quote: aiming to increase renewables' share of electricity consumption to 80% by 2030 to achieve a “largely climate neutral” power system by 2035
insights.locator: The nation is also aiming to increase renewables' share

insights.claim: Germany aims to install 115GW of onshore wind by 2030 and approved a record 20.8GW of new onshore wind capacity in 2025.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A record annual approval pace of 20.8GW is a concrete leading indicator for onshore wind equipment and construction demand in Germany through the rest of the decade.
insights.quote: Germany aims to install 115 gigawatts (GW) of onshore wind by 2030 and approved a record 20.8GW of new capacity in 2025.

insights.claim: Bioenergy, which is counted toward Germany's renewables targets alongside hydropower, supplied roughly a tenth of the country's electricity in 2025.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Bioenergy's meaningful ~10% contribution means Germany's renewables target is not solely a wind-and-solar story, which matters for anyone modeling the full power-mix composition.
insights.locator: The latter produces a relatively large share

insights.claim: Germany must lean more heavily on renewables than neighbors like France and the UK to hit its climate goals, because its 'Energiewende' strategy includes a full phaseout of nuclear power that those countries have not pursued.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Explains why Germany's renewables buildout pace needs to outstrip peer nations, raising the stakes of any slowdown in wind/solar deployment or grid-reform friction.
insights.locator: Germany has to rely on renewables more than neighbours

insights.claim: Chancellor Friedrich Merz called Germany's nuclear phaseout a 'strategic mistake' in 2026, yet his government has explicitly ruled out returning to conventional nuclear power.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Shows that even the sitting chancellor's public regret over the nuclear phaseout has not translated into policy reversal, reducing the odds of a near-term German nuclear restart.
insights.quote: described the nuclear phaseout as a “strategic mistake”
insights.locator: This year, the centre-right chancellor Friedrich Merz

insights.claim: Some commentators argue Germany could have cut coal generation even faster than it has if nuclear power had been retained rather than phased out alongside coal.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A live counterfactual debate worth tracking, since it could resurface as a political argument for slowing further nuclear-adjacent decommissioning or reshaping future energy policy.
insights.locator: While coal generation has fallen quickly

insights.claim: Germany's official coal phaseout deadline is 'no later than' 2038, but experts say the country is on track to eliminate coal from its power supply years ahead of that date, despite pressure to slow the transition during the recent energy crisis.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: An earlier-than-scheduled coal exit would accelerate stranded-asset risk for German coal generators and increase near-term reliance on gas and renewables to fill the gap.
insights.locator: The country has an official coal phaseout date of 2038

insights.claim: Renewables have faced growing opposition in Germany from the far-right AfD party, and the current coalition government under Merz has simultaneously been working to develop new gas-fired power plants.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Rising far-right political opposition to renewables plus government-backed gas expansion together represent a policy tailwind for gas developers and a risk factor for the pace of Germany's decarbonization.
insights.locator: Renewables have recently faced mounting opposition

insights.claim: Germany's government has adopted a law providing state support for new gas-fired power plants, framed as a bridge from coal and nuclear to a renewables-heavy grid, with the plants intended to convert to running on 'green hydrogen' by 2045 to meet the climate-neutrality goal.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: State-subsidized gas plants with a mandated hydrogen-conversion pathway create a concrete, trackable policy bet for hydrogen infrastructure and gas-turbine suppliers positioning for the 2045 deadline.
insights.quote: adopted a law to provide state support for new gas-fired power plants
insights.locator: The current government under Merz has tried to boost gas

insights.claim: The German government's planned grid reforms have drawn criticism from the renewables industry because, under the proposals, developers would only get automatic grid connections in limited-capacity areas if they waive compensation for future curtailed generation.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A compensation waiver requirement tied to grid access could depress returns for renewables developers in constrained-grid areas, a concrete risk factor for wind/solar project economics and financing terms.
insights.quote: renewables developers would only be granted automatic grid connections in areas with limited grid capacity if they waive compensation for future curtailed generation
insights.locator: the government's planned grid reforms have been criticised
